newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian premier sees low inflation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian premier sees low inflation.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Tuesday promised to bring inflation down next year and said the government would not give in to the temptation to loosen the monetary purse strings and print extra cash.

Chernomyrdin, speaking at the first autumn session of the Federation Council upper house of parliament, said year-on-year inflation should fall to 10 percent next year, from a likely 18-19 percent in 1996 and 130 percent in 1995.
The government would use "non-inflationary means" to cover the budget deficit, rather than printing money.
"There is no use asking us to switch on the printing presses," said Chernomyrdin, who is viewed by Western investors as the best guarantor of continued Russian economic reform.
"Doing so would bring short-term relief -- for a week, for a month -- but in the long run it will only make things worse."

The lower house of parliament is due to debate the 1997 budget on Friday and ministers have said they are determined to keep policy tight to ensure the International Monetary Fund pays out on a three-year $10 billion loan to Russia.
But tax evasion is a national sport in Russia and ministers are finding it hard to keep this year's budget on track.
"I once proposed an honorary decree declaring people hero taxpayers of the Russian Federation," Finance Minister Alexander Livshits told NTV commercial television on Monday.
"But it was turned down. These people would have become a laughing stock. No one would invite them for a shot of vodka."

The State Tax Service said on Tuesday that tax revenues fell almost 30 percent in September from August and were less than half the levels envisaged in the budget. Taxes were only 75 percent of budgeted levels in the first nine months.
But Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin told Prime-Tass news agency a new tax code would increase the chance of collecting taxes and he expected revenues to rise by October or November.
Chernomyrdin said Russia's key budget task was to raise revenues, because there was no way to cut spending further.
"Spending is a very important issue. It cannot be cut further but it should not be boosted either," he said.
He said Russia should look at a special tax to help fund the massive arrears of the cash-strapped armed forces but gave no details and said nothing had been agreed yet.

Many soldiers in the once-proud Russian army have not been paid for months and its facilities are neglected and run-down. Security chief Alexander Lebed, a reserve paratroop general, has said the army is close to mutiny.
"The government is taking measures to stabilise the situation," Chernomyrdin said.
He said the government would lower some prices for gas and electricity, a move which could make life easier for troubled domestic firms.
The new price structure could take effect as early as October 10, he said. Prices would be at least 10-15 percent lower than at the start of August.

The whole energy sector has been plagued by non-payments. Customers do not pay for energy they use and the energy companies do not pay their workers. Power workers went on strike in the Far East last month to complain about unpaid bills.
